cse-2007-cs-23.approach: A connected graph has an Eulerian circuit iff every vertex has even degree. Check degree parity and connectivity for each option.

steps.title: Criterion
steps.body: A graph (ignoring isolated vertices) has an Eulerian circuit $\iff$ it is **connected** and **every vertex has even degree**.

steps.title: Complement of $C_{25}$
steps.body:
In $C_{25}$ each vertex has degree 2, so in its complement each vertex has degree $(25-1)-2=22$, which is even.

The complement is connected: two vertices $u,v$ non-adjacent in $\overline{C_{25}}$ are adjacent in $C_{25}$, and any third vertex $w$ not adjacent (in $C_{25}$) to either of them — there are at least $25-4=21$ such — is a common neighbour in $\overline{C_{25}}$. So it has an Eulerian circuit.

steps.title: Other options
steps.body:
- $K_{90}$: every degree is $89$ (odd) — no.
- $k$-regular with even $k$: degrees are even but the graph may be **disconnected** (e.g. two disjoint triangles, $k=2$) — not guaranteed.

answer.value: The complement of a cycle on 25 vertices

optionAnalysis.reason: Even degrees alone are not enough; a disconnected 2-regular graph such as two disjoint triangles has no Eulerian circuit.
$K_{90}$ is 89-regular; odd degrees rule out an Eulerian circuit.
22-regular and connected, so an Eulerian circuit exists.

pitfalls: Forgetting the connectivity requirement in option A.
cse-2007-cs-23.verification: Degree $25-1-2=22$ is even; connectivity shown via a common neighbour.

cse-2007-cs-24.approach: Only the relative order of the 10 even numbers matters; by symmetry each of them is equally likely to come first among the evens.

steps.title: Reduce to the even numbers
steps.body: The evens are $2,4,\dots,20$ — 10 numbers. In a uniformly random permutation, their relative order is uniformly random over $10!$ orders.

steps.title: Probability
steps.body:
Each of the 10 evens is equally likely to appear first among them, so
$$P(2\text{ first among evens})=\frac{9!}{10!}=\frac{1}{10}.$$

optionAnalysis.reason: $\frac12$ would be right only if just two evens competed.
1 of 10 equally likely evens comes first.
$\frac{9!}{20!}$ is far too small; it ignores that the other 10 odd numbers are unconstrained.

cse-2007-cs-24.verification: Counting: choose positions for evens ($\binom{20}{10}$), place 2 in the earliest of them, arrange the other evens $9!$ and odds $10!$ ways: $\binom{20}{10}9!\,10!/20!=\frac{1}{10}$.

cse-2007-cs-28.approach: The iteration converges to a fixed point $x=\frac{x}{2}+\frac{9}{8x}$; solve for the positive root (start value is positive).

cse-2007-cs-31.approach: Simplify each language by taking $w$ to be a single symbol where possible. $wxw^R$ is exactly 'length $\ge3$, first symbol = last symbol', which is regular; the others need palindrome matching.

steps.title: Option C is regular
steps.body:
If $s=wxw^R$ with $w=a u$, then $s$ starts with $a$ and ends with $a$, and $|s|\ge3$.

Conversely, any $s=a\,y\,a$ with $|y|\ge1$ is $wxw^R$ with $w=a$, $x=y$.

So $L_C=0(0+1)^+0+1(0+1)^+1$ — **regular**.

steps.title: Option A is not regular
steps.body: $\{ww^R\}$ = even palindromes; the strings $0^n1$ are pairwise distinguishable by suffix $10^n$ (Myhill-Nerode), so not regular.

steps.title: Option B is not regular
steps.body: Take odd $k$ and prefixes $p_k=01^k00$. For odd $j$, $p_k1^j01$ belongs to $L_B$ iff it has a nonempty even-palindrome prefix followed by $\ge1$ more symbol. Such a prefix must begin and end with 0; the candidates $01^k0$ (odd length $k+2$) and $01^k00$ fail, so the only one is $01^k001^j0$, a palindrome iff $j=k$. Hence suffix $1^k01$ distinguishes $p_k$ from $p_{k'}$ ($k\ne k'$): infinitely many classes, **not regular**.

steps.title: Option D is not regular
steps.body: $xww^R$ = strings whose suffix (after a nonempty $x$) is an even palindrome. By the mirror of the argument for B (reverse all strings; regular languages are closed under reversal, and $(xww^R)^R=ww^Rx^R$), $L_D$ is not regular.

answer.keyNote: The stored key is B, but $\{ww^Rx\}$ is not regular (Myhill-Nerode argument in step 3), while $\{wxw^R\}$ equals the regular set of strings of length at least 3 whose first and last symbols agree. C is the widely accepted GATE 2007 answer.

optionAnalysis.reason: Requires recognising an even-palindrome prefix of unbounded length; infinitely many Myhill-Nerode classes.
Reverse of B's language, so also not regular.

pitfalls: Assuming B is regular by taking only $|w|=1$ — that gives a subset, not the whole language; longer $w$ adds strings like $0110\,1$ that do not start with $00$ or $11$.
cse-2007-cs-31.verification: For C, both inclusions were shown; for B, $0\,1^3\,00\,1^3\,0\,1\in L_B$ but $0\,1^1\,00\,1^3\,0\,1\notin L_B$.

cse-2007-cs-44.approach: This is Euclid's algorithm; the remainder at least halves every two steps (Lamé: worst case on consecutive Fibonacci numbers), so the number of calls is logarithmic.

steps.title: Halving argument
steps.body: For $n\ge m$: $n\bmod m<n/2$ (if $m\le n/2$ the remainder is $<m\le n/2$; otherwise it is $n-m<n/2$). Over two calls the first argument at least halves, so there are $O(\log_2 n)$ calls.

steps.title: Tight worst case
steps.body: For consecutive Fibonacci numbers $(F_{k+1},F_k)$ each step only drops one index, giving $k-1=\Theta(\log_\phi n)=\Theta(\log_2 n)$ calls. Hence $\Theta(\log_2 n)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Logarithmic bound, tight on Fibonacci inputs.
